title: Simmering weight broker and cache-simmer pipeline for rapid resume
creator: Samantha Li
description:
Goal: Implement a low-impact background "simmer" subsystem that keeps a lightweight subset of model weights and KV cache entries resident on dedicated fleet hosts so cold-start latency for bursty tenants is reduced without blocking throughput guarantees.

Problem statement: Current warm-pool priming loads full weight shards and larger KV seed sets during prewarm, which increases memory pressure and startup time. For workloads with sporadic bursts, full preloads are wasteful and still allow tail latency due to on-demand refills. We need a middle ground between cold (no state) and fully-warm (full weights + KV) that preserves capacity guarantees for committed tenants and reduces cold-start P90/P99.

Key idea: "Simmering" maintains compact, low-resolution representations of the most frequently-accessed weight slices (lightweight quantized micro-slices) and a thin KV footprint (hot keys only) that can accelerate the first 50-200 tokens of inference. The weight broker coordinates progressive upgrade: simmer -> quick-boost -> full-streaming. The broker runs at low IO priority and continuously opportunistically fills higher-fidelity state when load budget allows.

Acceptance criteria:
- Simmering keeps a measurable set of weight micro-slices and hot KV entries per tenant and reduces cold-start P99 by >= 35% for medium-length (200-800 tokens) requests in dedicated fleets (internal benchmark).
- Does not increase steady-state memory usage for a host by > 6% on average compared to baseline with warm-pool disabled (configurable per fleet).
- Integrates with autoscaler so that when traffic surge is detected the broker signals for fast-boost policy and the autoscaler can provision additional nodes within SLA windows.
- Has operational knobs: simmer size cap, hot-key retention window, IO niceness, and admission thresholds accessible via fleet config and console.

Non-goals: This ticket does not implement global model quantization changes or new kernel selection logic. It focuses on orchestration, lightweight representation, and admission controls.

Metrics to collect: simmer residency ratio, first-100-token latency delta, memory delta per-host, IO priority throttled bytes, number of quick-boost transitions per hour, and failed warmups.
implementation_plan: 1) Design data structures for micro-slices: define metadata, minimal float16/8 layout and precomputed stride indices. 2) Broker control plane: new lightweight controller in serving orchestrator to track simmer candidates and per-tenant budgets. 3) Local agent: low-priority background worker on host that performs streaming writes to local NVMe and maps micro-slices into local allocator. 4) KV simmer: adapt existing prefix caching to maintain 'hot-key' ring with eviction TTL and lightweight fingerprinting. 5) Autoscaler integration: extend surge policy to accept 'boost request' from broker and a quick-boost fast path to allocate staging nodes. 6) Feature gates + fleet config + console UI entries. 7) End-to-end stress tests and benchmark harness. 8) Phased rollout: internal dogfood -> opt-in customers -> default on small fleets.
risks: Risk: Micro-slice format mismatch across model revisions could cause incorrect outputs — mitigate with versioned checksum and model-compatibility checks
Risk: Background IO could affect hot inference — mitigate by IO niceness and pacing with CPU-aware backpressure
Risk: Increased operational complexity and harder debugging — mitigate by verbose observability and a debug mode that can replay transitions
rollout_plan:
- Stage 0: Unit tests and local dev harness (1 week).
- Stage 1: Canary on a single dedicated pool with low criticality tenants; monitor P50/P95/P99 and memory delta (2 weeks).
- Stage 2: Expand to multiple pools and enable quick-boost on opt-in customers (2 weeks).
- Stage 3: Wide release with defaults tuned and a toggle in console for fleet config (1 week).
acceptance_test_steps: Deploy canary branch to dedicated-canary pool
Run benchmark suite comparing baseline vs simmer enabled with synthetic burst traffic
Verify memory delta per host <= 6% and P99 reduced >= 35%
Trigger surge and confirm autoscaler responds to broker 'boost' within configured SLA
comments: 2025-02-11 Samantha Li: Initial spec drafted. Added micro-slice concept after discussion with Research. Confluence design: https://confluence.internal/redwood/simmering-design

2025-02-14 Ravi Menon: Design review notes — prefer strict version checks when mapping micro-slices to loaded weights. Also suggest a circuit breaker if quick-boost requests exceed allocation rate. Added to risks.
2025-02-18 Miguel Ortega (Infra): We need to ensure NVMe wear is considered for long-running simmer workloads; proposal to batch writes and use larger append windows.
2025-02-22 Engineering sync: Prototype local agent completed. Basic micro-slice format working. Observability hooks instrumented. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1124
2025-02-26 QA: Canary smoke shows P99 improvement ~28% (below target). Next actions: increase simmer budget on canary and test quick-boost trigger thresholds.
2025-02-28 Ravi Menon: Adjusted admission thresholds and added rate limiter on background IO. Preparing for Stage 1 canary run tomorrow.
notes: This ticket intentionally avoids renaming existing warm-pool primitives. 'Simmer' is a sibling subsystem that should be manageable with feature flags and clear operational defaults. Work needs close coordination with fleets and autoscaling owners to avoid resource thrash.
